result.reason: The passage directly addresses the question of whether ha'ada (warning) applies to tzroros-type damage, resolving it by explaining that the half-payment for pebbles reflects indirect/atypical action rather than unexpectedness, and then connects the dog-fire baraita to the Rabbi Tarfon vs. Rabbis dispute — exactly the thread that candidate 1 ('Sound as Kocho') establishes when it raises the ha'ada question and maps the two rulings onto yesh ha'ada l'tzroros vs. ein ha'ada l'tzroros.

All 10 items are the Gemara's sustained exploration of Rava's dilemma about whether there is ha'ada (forewarning) for tzroros, cycling through multiple attempted proofs (hopping chicken, excrement on dough, Rami bar Yechezkel's baraita about crowing/neighing) and rejecting each — exactly what the 'Review of Questions' prose describes as the central question of ha'ada for tzroros, not the 'Sound as Kocho' section which only covers items 7–10.

All three items form one continuous chain — Rav Ashi's dilemma about shinui l'tzroros (item 1), the attempted resolution from Rava's ha'ada question (item 2), and the rejection of that resolution via conditional logic (item 3) — which precisely matches the 'Shinui Question' prose describing Rav Ashi's question and its unresolved status, making the current placement correct.
Both items directly address Rav Ashi's dilemma about koach kocho l'Sumchus and whether it is treated like koach, ending in teiku — exactly what the 'Degrees of Removal' prose describes.

The passage quotes the mishna text about kicking and pebbles paying half damages, followed by the opening dilemma question, which matches precisely the 'Mishna Cases' section prose that introduces these two cases and notes the interpretive question the Gemara takes up.
The passage directly presents the two readings (rabbanan vs. Sumakhos) of the Mishnah regarding kicking and pebbles, which is precisely what the 'Two Readings' section prose describes.

All three items form a continuous Gemara sequence about the latter clause of the Mishnah (darsa al hakli), the possibility of reading it according to Sumakhos with koach vs. koach kocho, and Rav Ashi's unresolved dilemma — exactly what the 'Final Section' prose describes.

Both items are Rav Ashi's explicit dilemma about whether tzroros from kicking pays quarter or half and whether shinui applies to tzroros, concluding with teiku — exactly what candidate 1's prose describes in detail.

The passage is about Rabbi Abba bar Memel's dilemma concerning an animal walking where scattering is inevitable then kicking, which is precisely what the 'Inevitable Scatter' section's prose describes.

All 8 items form one continuous Talmudic exchange between Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Zeira about whether tzroros is a toldah of regel (exempt in reshus ha-rabim) or comparable to keren (liable), including the sub-question of hitiza be-reshus ha-rabim v'hizika be-reshus ha-yachid and Rabbi Zeira's repeated retractions — exactly the content described in the 'Regel Category' prose section.

Both items together present the initial tail-wagging dilemma and its immediate resolution (the 'must you hold its tail?' retort plus the keren/orchaya distinction), which is exactly what heading 0 'Tail Wagging' describes — the question posed by Rabbi Yehuda Nesia and Rabbi Oshaya about kishkeshah bi-znava — whereas the current placement under 'Natural Acts' (index 2) discusses the deeper irony and policy implications that follow from that resolution, not the dilemma itself.

The passage directly addresses the Gemara's question about excessive tail swinging (kishkush yeseirah), which is precisely what the 'Vigorous Wagging' section discusses, not the 'Two Rationales' section where it currently sits.
The passage is Rav Eina's dilemma about an animal swinging its penis and whether it constitutes keren, which is precisely what the 'Zoological Case' prose describes in detail.

All four items form a continuous chain: Rav Huna's ruling (item 1), the question of who pays when the string tangled on its own (item 2), the ish bor ve-lo shor bor objection to charging the chicken's owner (item 3), and the resolution that the mishna deals with addi aduyei while Rav Huna's ruling is about a hefker string (item 4) — this entire sequence matches the 'Negligent Placement' section's prose, which covers exactly the owner-of-string liability question, the anus/poshe'a distinction, the ela chayav ba'al ha-tarnagol move, and the ish bor ve-lo shor bor principle.
